sections.title: Passage 1 · Cooling cities without more air conditioning
sections.passage:
Cities are often warmer than the rural areas around them, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Roads, roofs and other dark surfaces absorb solar energy during the day and release it gradually after sunset. At the same time, dense buildings can reduce air movement, while traffic, industry and air-conditioning systems add waste heat. The result is not simply an uncomfortable afternoon. Higher night-time temperatures can prevent the human body from recovering after a hot day, increasing health risks during heatwaves.

One response is to increase tree cover. Trees intercept sunlight and cool the air through evapotranspiration, the movement of water from soil through plants into the atmosphere. Yet planting programmes are not automatically successful. Young trees need several years before their crowns provide substantial shade, and species that thrive in one climate may struggle in another. Roots can also conflict with underground utilities or narrow pavements. For these reasons, some cities map heat exposure, pedestrian activity and available soil before deciding where trees will provide the greatest benefit.

Cool roofs provide another strategy. A conventional dark roof may absorb a large proportion of incoming sunlight, whereas a reflective roof sends more radiation back into the atmosphere. The effect is strongest on the building itself: indoor temperatures and demand for mechanical cooling can fall. When reflective materials are installed across a large district, they may also reduce local air temperature slightly. However, the outcome depends on building type, climate and roof condition; a coating that performs well in a dry sunny region may deliver less value somewhere cloudy and cold.

A third approach is to redesign public space so that people can reach shade and water even before large infrastructure projects are completed. Temporary shade structures, drinking fountains and adjusted opening hours for public buildings can be deployed relatively quickly. Researchers increasingly argue that heat plans should combine these short-term protections with slower physical changes such as trees, roofs and redesigned streets. No single intervention removes urban heat. The strongest programmes treat heat as a system involving buildings, transport, public health and unequal exposure across neighbourhoods.

sections.title: Passage 2 · The return of repair
sections.passage:
For much of the twentieth century, household products became cheaper to replace and increasingly difficult to repair. Manufacturers often used sealed cases, proprietary fasteners and components that were glued rather than screwed together. At the same time, global supply chains lowered the retail price of many appliances. For a consumer facing a broken toaster or phone, purchasing a replacement could appear more rational than paying for diagnosis, labour and spare parts.

That calculation is now being challenged. Repair cafés, community workshops and online repair communities have expanded in many countries. Their supporters describe repair not only as a way to reduce waste but also as a means of preserving practical knowledge. A volunteer who helps someone replace a laptop battery may also teach safe tool use, fault diagnosis and the confidence to attempt future maintenance. This educational role helps explain why community repair events continue even when the financial saving on a single item is small.

Policy is changing too. Some jurisdictions have introduced or proposed ‘right to repair’ rules requiring manufacturers to provide spare parts, manuals or diagnostic information for a defined period. The details vary widely. A rule covering washing machines may not apply to smartphones, and access to a part does not guarantee that it will be affordable. Manufacturers also raise legitimate concerns about safety, cybersecurity and intellectual property, particularly when repairs involve batteries, medical devices or network-connected products.

Researchers therefore caution against treating repairability as a simple yes-or-no feature. A product can be physically opened yet remain impractical to fix because replacement parts are expensive or software refuses to recognise them. Conversely, a sealed component may be replaced safely as a complete module. Several proposed repairability labels attempt to capture multiple factors: availability of documentation, price of parts, ease of disassembly and expected software support.

The environmental case is similarly nuanced. Extending product life usually avoids the material and energy required to manufacture a replacement. But keeping an extremely inefficient old appliance in service may consume more energy than replacing it with a much more efficient model. The most useful question is therefore not ‘repair or replace?’ in isolation. It is how product design, energy use, part availability and expected remaining life interact in a particular case.

sections.title: Passage 3 · When scientific teams become larger
sections.passage:
Scientific papers increasingly list more authors than they did several decades ago. In some fields, a study may require expertise in statistics, laboratory methods, field sampling, software engineering and specialist equipment. Large collaborations can make projects possible that no individual laboratory could complete alone. Astronomy offers a striking example: major observatories generate data used by teams spread across many institutions and countries. Similar patterns occur in genomics, climate science and large clinical studies.

Team growth, however, changes how credit is allocated. Traditional author lists suggest a simple sequence, with the first author often associated with much of the practical work and the final author with senior supervision. That convention becomes less informative when dozens or hundreds of researchers contribute distinct forms of expertise. Some journals now ask authors to describe contributions using standard categories such as data curation, software, methodology, visualisation and project administration. Supporters argue that these statements make otherwise invisible work easier to recognise.

Large teams may also influence the kind of research that gets produced. Studies comparing publication patterns have reported that small teams are more likely to introduce ideas that disrupt established lines of work, while large teams more often develop and extend existing directions. One explanation is organisational: coordinating many people encourages clear milestones and lowers tolerance for projects whose outcome is highly uncertain. Another explanation concerns resources. Large teams frequently work on expensive programmes that already have defined objectives. These findings do not mean that large teams are uncreative or that small teams are always radical; they describe statistical tendencies across many projects.

Communication presents another challenge. Adding experts does not automatically combine their knowledge. Specialists may use the same word differently, assume unfamiliar background knowledge, or optimise for different goals. Successful collaborations therefore invest in shared documentation, regular cross-disciplinary meetings and people who can translate between domains. Software tools can help, but organisational practices remain important.

There is also a career dimension. Early-career researchers can gain access to equipment, data and mentors through large projects, yet their individual contribution may be difficult for hiring committees to identify. Contribution statements, open code repositories and clearly owned sub-projects can provide stronger evidence of what a researcher actually did. For institutions, the challenge is to reward both the visible intellectual leadership of a paper and the less visible technical work that makes complex research reliable.

The debate is sometimes framed as a choice between the agility of small teams and the power of large ones. In practice, scientific ecosystems need both. Small groups may explore uncertain ideas cheaply; successful directions can later attract larger collaborations capable of testing them at scale. Rather than asking for an ideal team size, research organisations may gain more by matching team structure to the stage and demands of a problem.
